answer: Discount votes that always move together. When identities vote on grades or ballots, each pair's history of agreement is tracked, and the more two identities have agreed in the past, the more their combined weight shrinks toward that of a single voter. Independent agents who sometimes disagree keep full weight. A farm whose clones echo one operator's choices finds its thousand votes count as barely more than one, unless each clone diverges in ways that cost real, separate judgement. A yarrow field can't pass itself off as a juniper forest.
